title: Charge carriers change when an ionic material melts
stem: A dry binary material contains ions M²⁺ and X⁻. The graph shows current at equal voltages for its solid and molten states. The melt conducts, while the intact solid does not. Decomposition and chemical reactions at the electrodes are excluded from this comparison. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce the empirical formula and describe the solid’s bonding model.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the change in conductivity on melting and identify the moving charge carriers.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student claims melting must turn MX₂ into neutral M and X₂. Evaluate that claim using the observations and atom/charge accounting.

steps.text: Neutrality requires two X⁻ ions per M²⁺.
Formula MX₂.
A giant ionic lattice contains oppositely charged ions held by electrostatic attractions in all directions.
In the solid the ions occupy fixed lattice positions and cannot migrate through the material.
Melting allows ions to move under the applied field.
Both cations and anions carry charge; the explanation does not require free electrons as in a metal.
Melting is a physical loss of lattice order and does not itself discharge the ions.
Neutral M and X₂ would require electron transfer, not just ion movement.
The conductivity evidence is consistent with mobile M²⁺ and X⁻, not proof of formation of neutral elements.

title: Inferring an ionic formula and lattice-strength comparison
stem: Ion A contains12 protons and 10 electrons; ion B contains8 protons and 10 electrons. A schematic lattice slice is shown. Ionic radii are A: 72 pm, B: 140 pm, Na⁺: 102 pm, Cl⁻: 181 pm. Compare attraction qualitatively; no lattice-enthalpy calculation is required. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the ions, their charges and the neutral formula.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Predict whether MgO or NaCl should have stronger electrostatic lattice attractions, using both charge and size.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why ions being isoelectronic does not make them identical particles or force equal ionic radii.

steps.text: Charge is proton count minus electron count.
A isMg²⁺ and B isO²⁻; formula MgO.
Each ion has10 electrons, a neon-like electron configuration.
Mg²⁺/O²⁻ have larger charge magnitudes than Na⁺/Cl⁻.
The supplied Mg²⁺/O²⁻ radii also give a smaller interionic separation.
Both factors support stronger attractions in MgO and a generally higher melting temperature.
Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have different nuclear proton numbers, 12 and 8.
With the same electron count, the greater nuclear attraction in Mg²⁺ draws its electron cloud in more strongly.

title: Why a shifted ionic layer fractures rather than flows
stem: The diagram is a schematic ionic lattice slice after its lower rows have shifted relative to the upper rows. Compare it with a metal whose positive cores remain immersed in delocalized electrons when rows shift. Unless stated otherwise, retain unrounded working and give calculated non-exact numerical results to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain the mechanical consequence of the ionic layer shift.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the corresponding shift is compatible with metallic malleability.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare electrical conductivity of the intact ionic solid and the metal, naming carriers in each.

steps.text: The shift brings some like-charged ions into closer opposition.
Repulsion between like charges can split the crystal.
The ionic solid is brittle rather than generally malleable.
Metallic attraction is between positive cores and a shared delocalized electron population.
It is not a set of directional localized bonds that must all break on sliding.
The electron population can continue attracting the shifted cores.
The metal conducts through mobile delocalized electrons.
In the ionic solid the ions are fixed; neither a mobile ion population nor metallic delocalized electrons is available.

title: An ether can accept water hydrogen bonds without self-donating
stem: The structures are ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, and dimethyl ether, CH₃OCH₃. Both have molar mass46.0 g mol⁻¹. Their boiling points are78 °C and−24 °C respectively. A waterO–H group donates a hydrogen bond to an etherO lone pair.

Mobile delocalized electrons carry charge through the solid.
